Abstract

blocks.text: Deploying LLM agents typically requires a compact test-time student, even if a stronger teacher is available during training. We study knowledge brewing: distilling a teacher’s interactive experience into a persistent external memory for the student. Crucially, this requires no weight updates, expert demonstrations, ground-truth labels, or test-time teacher access. This setting poses two challenges: environments provide only sparse, binary feedback, and teacher-authored notes must be inherently tailored to be concretely executable by a substantially weaker student. To address these hurdles, we proposeAgentBrew, comprising two coupled components. First, a failure-triggered teacher–Ralph Loop mitigates sparse feedback by transforming student failures into environment-validated notes. Second, student-aware synthesis calibrates teacher knowledge to the weak executor’s operational granularity, yielding model-specific, actionable guidance. Extensive evaluations and comprehensive ablations across coding, math, and tool-use tasks demonstrate that this asymmetric, training-free brewing paradigm produces highly capable yet deployable LLM agents.

Introduction

blocks.text: Large language model (LLM) agents now solve interactive tasks in coding, math, and tool-use environments [1–4]. In production, however, the agent that must serve requests is often a small or API-only model: fine-tuning may be unavailable, inference cost must stay low, and model weights are treated as fixed after deployment. A natural alternative is teacher–student agent brewing1: a stronger teacher agent T (large LLM) distills interaction experience during a training period, while a compact student agent S (small LLM) runs alone at test time with only retrieved external knowledge. The central question is how to convert brewing-time interaction into durable notes that raise S’s effective capability without updating its parameters. Two challenges make this setting substantially harder than either self-evolution or standard distillation alone.Challenge I: sparse environment feedback.Real benchmarks and deployed APIs typically expose only a terminal binary rewardR∈ {0,1}—pass or fail—together with the agent’s own rollout, but no ground-truth solution, expert trajectory, or step-level label. When S fails, the only extra signal is the failure trajectory τS (x); when it succeeds, no teacher intervention is needed.Challenge II: teacher–student capability gap (i.e., knowledge is model-specific).In the deployment scenario above, T is intentionally much stronger than S, yet the notes stored in memory must be written by T and executed by S. Existing work addresses only parts of the problem. Self-evolving agents [5, 6] can improve from environment feedback without weight updates, but they usually (i) evolve the same model that both acts and learns, (ii) continue adapting at test time, and (iii) are not built for asymmetric teacher-student "brewing", where notes must be validated for a fixed weak executor. Agent distillation [7, 8] can compress teacher behavior into trajectories or reusable artifacts, but it typically depends on labeled pairs or successful teacher rollouts, and it transfers knowledge at a teacher-level abstraction rather than as student-executable notes certified to work on the weak executor. Accordingly, we organize our investigation around three questions: Q1 (Learning signal).When Env exposes only binary R and no expert data, how can a weak agent extract useful knowledge from failures, and how can we verify that knowledge before storing it? Q2 (Capability gap).How can a strong teacher author knowledge that a substantially weaker student can execute—not merely parse—given that both generation and validation are biased by the gap? Q3 (Lifelong accumulation).How can validated, student-calibrated knowledge accumulate across tasks in external memory-without updating student weights S-while keeping test-time inference lightweight and stable? We call itAgentBrew:brewingis the Ralph Loop [ 9] that iteratively distills certified notes from failures, and student-aware synthesis tailors each note to its executor as a brewer adapts method to the ingredients. Brewing on Dtrain proceeds as follows. Student S rolls out each task in Env; when R=0, teacher T reads (x, τS (x))—the only supervision beyond binary pass/fail—and drafts a structured candidate note. The note is authored with student-aware prompting and an action-oriented schema so that T targets S’s reading level and operational granularity rather than its own. The Ralph Loop then stages the note and re-rolls S on the same task: recovery (R=1) certifies the note using environment feedback alone, and rejects guidance that remains plausible to T yet unusable for the weak executor. A curator deduplicates certified notes and appends them to M, which grows across the training stream without updating S. Serving on Dtest reads from frozen M⋆: T is inactive, S retrieves skill-scoped top-k notes, and completes each task in a single rollout with no iterative reflection or online memory writes. AgentBrew is guided by a simple principle:knowledge is not universal—it must fit the agent that executes it. blocks.text: Setup.We examine interactive tasks x (e.g.,math, coding, or tool-use). A fixed student agent S, powered by a small LLM, interacts with an environment Env for up to H steps to yield a trajectory τS (x) and a binary terminal reward R(x, τ)∈0,1 . During training (Dtrain), a stronger teacher agent T , driven by a large LLM, is introduced: upon any failure by S, T analyzes the task and the failed trajectory to synthesize structured notes into an external memory bank M. During testing ( Dtest), M is frozen and T is entirely absent; instead, S solves tasks in a single pass augmented by notes retrieved from M. Overall, learning is driven purely by environment feedback and failure trajectories, without offline demonstrations, test-time oracle labels, or updates to the parameters ofS. blocks.text: AgentBrew operationalizes the objective in Sec. 2.1 via abrew–serveparadigm (Figure 2): The full system comprises three design choices, each addressing a research question raised in the introduction: (Q1)a failure-triggeredteacherturns sparse binary feedback from Env into structured candidate notes, with acuratormerging environment-certified entries into M (Sec. 2.3);(Q2) reactive Ralph validationplusproactive student-aware synthesisbridge the capability gap between teacher and student agents (Sec. 2.4); and(Q3)alifelong memory M accumulates validated notes across tasks without updating the student LLM (Sec. 2.5). Here we summarize how they interact: • Brewing phase(on Dtrain).For each task x, the student agent S attempts x in Env. If R=1, the teacher is not invoked and the pipeline advances to the next task. If R=0, the teacher agent T reads (x, τS (x)) and, via student-aware prompting, proposes a structured candidate note n. The Ralph Loop [9] injects n into S and re-rolls out on thesametask x: a successful re-rollout (R=1) validates n, whereas persistent failure triggers revision or discard. Notes that pass the Ralph Loop are merged by a curator agent—performing deduplication and quality gating only, as correctness is already certified by the environment—and appended to M. This cycle repeats over the training stream, progressively brewingM ⋆. • Serving phase(on Dtest).At test time, memory is read-only and the teacher agent T is inactive. Structured Note Generation

blocks.text: Given a failure, T outputs a candidate note n as structured JSON rather than a worked example. Each note is an abstract, reusable rule intended for retrieval on future tasks with similar structure: •note_key: unique identifier (reused when updating an existing rule); •trigger_pattern: task features that should activate the note; •corrective_rule: an executable fix directive forS; •minimal_steps: a short ordered checklist lowering interpretation cost for a weak LLM; •tags: domain or skill labels for routing; •quality_score: initial confidence, later updated from validation statistics. Notes deliberately avoid storing full solutions to x; they compress failures into transferable guardrails. Granularity and wording are calibrated to the student agent’s capability.

Bridging the Capability Gap

blocks.text: Teacher agent T is substantially stronger than student agent S, leading to the capability gap [ 10] between to agents. We addressQ2with atwo-stagedesign.First, reactive validation: the Ralph Loop[ 9] re-rolls S on the failed task with a candidate note staged in memory and accepts n only when Env returns R=1, using terminal reward—not teacher or student self-judgment—as the certification signal.Second, proactive synthesis: student-aware prompting and note schema calibrate what T writes before validation, so proposals match S’s reading level and operational granularity. Ralph provides the environment-grounded filter; proactive synthesis improves validation yield and transferability. • Why same-level generation fails.Prior work on knowledge transfer, such as ACE [ 11], assumes that the knowledge producer and consumer have comparable reasoning ability. When T is substantially stronger than S, this assumption breaks down [12, 13]: notes often omit intermediate reasoning, use mismatched vocabulary, or specify steps at a granularity too coarse for S to follow. Such notes may appear plausible toTyet leaveSunable to recover.

blocks.text: AgentBrew addressesQ3by treating external memory M as the sole durable state: validated notes accumulate across Dtrain, and student agent S reads from a frozen M⋆ at test time. No gradient updates or adapter weights are applied; effective capability grows becauseM grows. We structure M to limit cross-domain interference, append new knowledge without erasing old entries, and retrieve notes with a serving pipeline tuned for single-pass inference.

Skill-Scoped Memory Architecture

blocks.text: A monolithic note pool inducescross-scope interference: notes from one skill are retrieved on unrelated tasks. We therefore partition M into disjoint skill scopes {Ms}s∈S, each indexing notes for a single capability or environment slice. Every note stores tags and an optional scope identifier; during curation, the teacher writes it to the corresponding Ms. At test time, retrieval first selects a scope subsetM scope ⊆ Mand ranks notes only within that subset-never over the full pool. Scope routing is orthogonal to note ranking. When x does not clearly specify a scope, we choose Mscope using three signals, in order:(i)explicit scope or tool names in x;(ii)lexical or semantic similarity between x and a scope-description catalog maintained alongside M;(iii)actions observed in the student rolloutτ S (x)when (i)–(ii) are inconclusive. 6

Continual Accumulation and Stability

blocks.text: During brewing, accepted notes are merged withappend-onlysemantics: curator deduplication mayupdatean existing note_key, but validated rules are never deleted to make room for new ones, avoiding catastrophic forgetting of earlier skills. Each note record tracks usage statistics and quality_score so frequently harmful or redundant entries can be down-weighted at retrieval time without erasing history. Train and test streams are strictly separated. While processing Dtrain, M is writable. On Dtest, M⋆ isfrozen read-only: no teacher calls, no provisional writes, and no statistic updates that leak test-task content back into the store. This guarantees that performance on held-out tasks measures generalization from brewed knowledge, not online adaptation to test labels or test-task feedback.

blocks.text: Serving reuses the objective in Eq. 1 with a fixed retrieval-and-rollout procedure (Appendix A.1). Given task x, we encode a queryq(x) from the instruction, select the skill scope, and retrieve candidate notes fromM ⋆ scope using dense or hybrid lexical–semantic scoring. Candidates are reranked by score(n, x) = sim(q(x), n)·ρ(n)·ϕ(n),(3) where sim(·) is retrieval similarity, ρ(n) is the stored quality_score (and success-rate prior), and ϕ(n) is a frequency penalty that down-weights notes over-selected in past tasks to promote diversity. Rather than hard-dropping low-scoring notes,soft suppressionapplies ϕ(n) and a relative-score floor: notes below a fraction of the top score are dampened but may still appear when the pool is sparse, reducing brittle all-or-nothing retrieval. The top-k notes are formatted and prepended to S’s prompt; S then performs one ROLLOUT in Env. If retrieval returns an empty set, S falls back to its vanilla policy with no memory augmentation.

Tasks and Benchmarks

blocks.text: We evaluate AgentBrew across three representative agent scenarios—coding,math, andtool-use— each probing a distinct capability profile: synthesizing executable programs from natural-language specifications, performing multi-step symbolic reasoning, and completing long-horizon tasks through interactive API calls. More details are in App. A.2. • For thecodingtasks, we evaluate AgentBrew onMBPP[ 14], a benchmark of roughly 1,000 entry-level Python programming tasks, andMBPP+[ 15], an extension that applies stricter unit testing to a curated subset to reduce spurious passes. • For themathtasks, we evaluate AgentBrew onMATH[ 16], comprising challenging competitionlevel problems, andGSM8K[ 17], which tests multi-step grade-school arithmetic reasoning. We score final-answer accuracy using the Qwen2.5-Math [18] evaluation framework. • For thetool-usetasks, we evaluate AgentBrew onAppWorld[ 2], an interactive benchmark where agents write and execute Python code to complete realistic, multi-app daily tasks in a simulated environment with multiple APIs.

Self-Improving Agents from Environment Feedback

blocks.text: LLM agents interleave language reasoning with environment actions (e.g., ReAct [21] and Toolformerstyle tool-use [27]). Beyond one-shot prompting, a self-evolving agent literature studies how agents improve from interaction rather than offline expert labels, often leveraging sparse environment feedback as the main supervision for accumulating reusable competence [28]. Representative approaches differ in what they evolve and what feedback they require: verbal self-improvement systems treat language as mutable memory by writing critiques after failures (e.g., Reflexion [5] and Self-Refine [29]), while experience-driven skill libraries extract reusable procedures from interaction to grow pools or code-based repositories (e.g., ExpeL [ 6] and V oyager [30]). More modular self-evolution and long-horizon memory frameworks push adaptation toward reusable protocols or persistent external stores (e.g., Alita [31] and OMNE [32]), and playbook-style context engineering closes executionreflection-curation loops by revising structured bullets (e.g., ACE [11]). Overall, most self-evolving agents assume same-capability evolution and adapt online at test time, learning from successes or rich feedback, whereas AgentBrew instead performs offline "brewing" of environment-validated, student-aware notes under binary supervision only, and then serves them via a frozen memory at test time.

Knowledge Transfer and Lifelong Memory for LLM Agents

blocks.text: Knowledge distillation has been widely used to compress large language models and has recently been extended to agent settings by transferring behavior from a teacher to a student across different transfer channels [33, 34]. At the trajectory level, structured span supervision and retrieval-augmented rollouts train students to imitate interleaved reasoning-action traces [7, 35]. In contrast, structure-level distillation compresses trajectories into interaction graphs or subgoal plans to preserve high-level task structure [36, 37]. Training-free approaches further store reusable external artifacts: for example, AgentDistill extracts Model-Context-Protocols (MCPs) from successful teacher trajectories into an inference-time MCP-Box [8]. RAG Distillation similarly distill teacher-to-student knowledge from failure-extracted hints, but internalize it into model weights via fine-tuning at the teacher’s abstraction level, without calibrating knowledge to the student’s capability or supporting incremental accumulation without re-training [38]. Related memory-based and lifelong-retrieval settings maintain external knowledge without parameter updates [ 32, 39, 40, 2].Overall, our work addresses the limitations of protocol-like artifact transfer and teacher-dependent abstractions by generating studentvalidated corrective notes from student failures using only binary rewards.

Conclusion

blocks.text: We study a practical deployment scenario for LLM agents where a strong teacher is available during training but only a fixed, weaker student serves at test time—with no weight updates, no teacher access, and only binary pass/fail feedback. The core challenge is that teacher knowledge, however insightful, often fails when executed by a substantially weaker student. We introduced AgentBrew, a training-free brew–serve framework built on the principle that knowledge must be calibrated to its executor. Its three components directly address the key obstacles: a failure-triggered teacher with Ralph Loop validation converts sparse binary feedback into environment-certified notes (Q1); studentaware synthesis paired with reactive validation bridges the teacher–student capability gap (Q2); and an append-only skill-scoped memory accumulates knowledge across tasks without modifying the student model (Q3). Extensive experiments across coding, math, tool-use, and a real-world Terminal-Bench deployment demonstrate that AgentBrew consistently lifts a fixed weak student, surpassing teacher-agnostic memory baselines. 12

The skill-scoped router ROUTESCOPE then selects a partition Mscope ⊆ M⋆ following the scoping policy in Sec. 2.5.1—explicit scope hints in x are matched first, then lexical similarity against category descriptions, and finally runtime cues when available—confining subsequent retrieval to a relevant skill subset and preventing cross-domain interference (line 3). For computational efficiency during brewing, we only use the first 1,000 problems from their official train splits. For evaluation, we use the complete official test splits (5,000 for MATH and 1,319 for GSM8K), reporting accuracy under symbolic equivalence checking. Coding.We build on the sanitized MBPP benchmark (427 Python tasks), which is a subset of the original MBPP corpus (∼500/500 train/test partition). Following the standard convention, we use tasks with task_id∈[11,510] for train (257 tasks) and task_id>510 for test (163 tasks). MBPP+ extends MBPP with stronger tests (378 tasks) but provides no explicit train/test split. Thus, we construct a strictly held-out test set by filtering out all MBPP+ tasks whose IDs overlap with our MBPP train split, retaining 154 tasks for evaluation. We report Pass@1 using native assertions for MBPP and EvalPlus tests for MBPP+. Tool-use.AppWorld originally provides 729 interactive API tasks partitioned into train (90 tasks), dev (57), test_normal (168), and test_challenge (417). We directly brew on the official train split and evaluate on the two official test splits of increasing difficulty: test_normal and test_challenge. We report Task Goal Completion (TGC) over tasks and Scenario Goal Completion (SGC). 17
